title: Third-Party Service Integrations
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of third-party service integrations and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to third-party service integrations.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on third-party service integrations. Third-party integrations should scope credentials, validate outgoing payloads, use timeouts and retry rules, and document provider availability/rate limits. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Third-Party Service Integrations matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Third-party integrations should scope credentials, validate outgoing payloads, use timeouts and retry rules, and document provider availability/rate limits. External integrations need explicit authentication, narrow permissions, input validation, rate-limit handling, deduplication, and safe reporting that does not leak credentials or payloads.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Third-party integrations should scope credentials, validate outgoing payloads, use timeouts and retry rules, and document provider availability/rate limits. External integrations need explicit authentication, narrow permissions, input validation, rate-limit handling, deduplication, and safe reporting that does not leak credentials or payloads. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Cloud services

items.title: Code quality and security platforms
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

items.title: Deployment systems
items.text: For deployment systems, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Secret managers
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

items.title: Integration permissions and trust evaluation
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

content_blocks.code:
name: Call an external service safely
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  call-service:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Request service status
        env:
          SERVICE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SERVICE_TOKEN }}
          SERVICE_URL: ${{ vars.SERVICE_STATUS_URL }}
        run: curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 15 -H "Authorization:Bearer $SERVICE_TOKEN" "$SERVICE_URL"
content_blocks.expected_output: The request fails on an unsuccessful HTTP response and times out rather than waiting forever; configure the token and URL in protected settings.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use only a test endpoint authorized for the exercise. Confirm the response does not contain sensitive information before logging it.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Never echo the token, append it to a URL, or run arbitrary shell text supplied by the external service.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to third-party service integrations. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain third-party service integrations, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Use GitHub APIs and CLI integration with explicit authentication, bounded permissions, and handled failures.

content.task: Apply third-party service integrations to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Third-party integrations should scope credentials, validate outgoing payloads, use timeouts and retry rules, and document provider availability/rate limits.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Third-party integrations should scope credentials, validate outgoing payloads, use timeouts and retry rules, and document provider availability/rate limits. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Third-party integrations should scope credentials, validate outgoing payloads, use timeouts and retry rules, and document provider availability/rate limits.
External integrations need explicit authentication, narrow permissions, input validation, rate-limit handling, deduplication, and safe reporting that does not leak credentials or payloads.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
